extracted.intended_audience: fiction writers and storytellers (writers thinking about cast/ensemble and genre expectations)
extracted.subtask_description: Advice on how the choice of genre shapes the structure, interactions, and use of an ensemble cast, including when to use single POV vs multiple POVs and how to meet or subvert genre expectations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Learn and deliver on genre expectations for ensembles
rubrics_metrics.description: The genre you choose can greatly affect what kinds of ensembles you have and what kinds of groups of characters you have.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Understand the trappings and expectations of the genre you’re working in so you deliver what readers expect (or intentionally subvert it). Example: Avengers (superhero genre) maps by-the-numbers to deliver fan expectations; Oceans (heist genre) follows heist conventions. If you fail to deliver required genre elements, readers may feel the story isn't really that genre.

rubrics_metrics.name: Superhero-genre requirement: heroes must test powers against each other
rubrics_metrics.description: In the superhero genre there is an expectation that at some point, every hero will test their powers against every other hero.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If writing a superhero ensemble, include inter-hero conflicts/tests (e.g., Thor vs Iron Man) because fans expect the 'matrix' of interactions. Use this as a checklist when constructing scenes and character interactions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Heist-genre convention: ensemble teammates don't fight each other for spectacle
rubrics_metrics.description: Heist films do not typically have the leader fight every member of the team; that kind of inter-team combat is not part of the heist genre's expectations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid gratuitous intra-team fights that would feel out of place in a heist story. Let heist ensembles focus on complementary skills and coordinated action rather than spectacle fights among teammates.

rubrics_metrics.name: Single-POV expectation in thrillers/detective stories
rubrics_metrics.description: Detective stories and thrillers often are single-point, one POV stories rather than ensembles.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If you’re writing a thriller or detective story, consider keeping to one protagonist viewpoint to preserve tension and focus; additional helpers should support the protagonist rather than become a competing ensemble.

rubrics_metrics.name: Fantasy/epic tendency toward multiple POVs or ensembles
rubrics_metrics.description: Fantasy and epics frequently are big, sprawling works with multiple POVs and may be ensembles (e.g., Fellowship of the Ring) or simply many distinct POVs.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When writing fantasy/epics, plan for balancing multiple character arcs and ensuring each POV contributes to the larger narrative. Decide whether the multiple POVs form an interacting ensemble or are loosely connected vignettes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition of ensemble: intersecting relationships and individual goals
rubrics_metrics.description: A true ensemble implies that members all intersect and each has their own goals and relationships with the others (illustrated with the love-triangle example).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ensure ensemble members have relationships among themselves (not just all tied to a single protagonist). If characters do not meaningfully interact with each other, you may not have an ensemble but separate supporting roles.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ensemble as found family and tone implications
rubrics_metrics.description: Ensembles are often 'found family' with family dynamics; the choice of tone (e.g., warm banter vs high tension) affects how that family functions in the story.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Decide whether ensemble dynamics should provide safety/comfort (reducing tension) or be used as leverage (threaten or endanger members to raise stakes). Use ensemble relationships to achieve your chosen tone.

rubrics_metrics.name: Using ensemble to raise tension by threatening members
rubrics_metrics.description: You can create fear/tension either by isolating a character (single-POV danger) or by putting the people who matter to them in danger.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If you want emotional stakes, threaten ensemble members rather than (or in addition to) the protagonist; this leverages the found-family bond to produce powerful emotional responses.

rubrics_metrics.name: Tone decides how much ensemble comfort to present
rubrics_metrics.description: If you want a tense, frightening adventure, you may need to reduce the safety or comfort of the ensemble; conversely, for comedic or exploratory adventures you may rely on ensemble camaraderie.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Match your ensemble’s level of safety and interdependence to the tone you aim for; adjust cast size, roles, and relationships accordingly.

rubrics_metrics.name: Respect subgenre-specific rules (cozy mystery example)
rubrics_metrics.description: Different subgenres carry explicit rules—for example, in cozy mysteries 'the detective is never actually threatened' and 'we don’t actually see violence committed.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Read and internalize subgenre rules; changing your approach to fit those expectations can fix scenes that feel off. If you want to blend genres, be deliberate about which rules you keep or discard.

rubrics_metrics.name: Cultural expectations shape ensemble style
rubrics_metrics.description: Cultural conventions influence whether stories favor lone heroes (Western action one-on-one showdowns) or group collaboration (many Hong Kong action films involve teams).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consider cultural storytelling traditions that influence audience expectations and adjust whether your cast acts as lone avenger or cooperative unit.

rubrics_metrics.name: Blend ensemble with other elemental genres deliberately
rubrics_metrics.description: An ensemble (an 'elemental genre') can be blended with other genres (sense of wonder, suspense/thriller, cozy, etc.).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When blending, identify which elemental conventions are essential and how the ensemble will express them. Use prior analyses of the elemental genres to guide structural choices.

rubrics_metrics.name: Practical casting changes when changing genre
rubrics_metrics.description: When imagining your work-in-progress as a different genre, consider how your cast or ensemble would need to change—create an ensemble, promote side characters, or demote mains.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Perform the homework thought experiment: change genre and then reassign roles, adjust POV distribution, and alter relationships to fit the new genre’s expectations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Promise of the premise: set and fulfill expectations
rubrics_metrics.description: Everything boils down to the promise of the premise—readers/listeners come in expecting certain things from a genre and you must meet (or knowingly subvert) those promises.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Identify the core promise your premise makes and ensure your ensemble structure helps fulfill that promise; if you subvert expectations, do so intentionally and provide satisfying reasons.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid genre-incongruous spectacle
rubrics_metrics.description: Do not introduce spectacles or mechanics (like unnecessary fights between teammates) that are incongruous with the genre's conventions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ask whether each set-piece or interpersonal beat serves the genre's expectations or your deliberate subversion; cut or rework elements that feel shoehorned-in.
